# Abstract

Operation Viscount Project CASTLE reconstructs the long-run demographic, settlement and spatial history of the Japanese archipelago and the Korean peninsula from 10000BC to 2026AD across thirteen integrated regional modules and four major chronological sections. Enclosing a contiguous domain of 617.753 km² across insular Japan (390.852 km²) and peninsular Korea (226.901 km²), CASTLE establishes a unified non-stationary Matérn geostatistical architecture with smoothness parameter $\nu = 3/2$. This spatial substratum anchors 103.888 composite archaeological and historical site-epoch observations across nine Holocene horizons onto 383 active domestic catchments out of 384 HydroBASINS Level 6 hydrological units. Across 9.224 valid terrestrial cells on the global 5-arcminute grid, the model attains regularised variogram parameters of $\tau_1 = 1,4211$ and $\tau_2 = 2,6291$, a median Voronoi catchment radius of 25,09 km, suppresses uninhabitable alpine crags with zero wasteland leakage, and resolves settlement concentrations along alluvial corridors and marine coasts without jurisdictional seam tears.

Section 1 traces Holocene hunter-gatherer and early farming adaptations across prehistoric Korea and Japan from 10000BC to 250BC. Beginning from initial post-glacial forager bands of 32k across the combined domain in 10000BC, populations expand through Middle Jomon and Chulmun pottery cultures to a mid-Holocene climatic optimum of 371k around 3000BC (Japan 261k, Korea 110k). Following a cooling contraction near 2000BC (310k), Mumun intensive dry-field farming, bronze metallurgy and megalithic dolmen building carry peninsular population to 700k by 250BC, while Final Jomon communities in western Japan prepare for the arrival of continental wet-rice agriculture (120k). Sections 2 and 3 trace dynastic state formation, mediaeval transformations and early modern consolidation across Japan and Korea. In Japan, Yayoi wet-rice expansion into northern Kyushu, Setouchi and Kinai leads into the Kofun tumulus state (expanding from 120k at 250BC to 4,5M at 650AD), Asuka-Nara Ritsuryo administration, the severe 735AD-737AD smallpox epidemic crash (reducing Japanese population from 5,4M to 4M), Heian court stability, Kamakura double-cropping agrarian revolutions, and Sengoku urban consolidation (reaching 12,27M by 1603AD). Under the Pax Tokugawa, population surges to 31,28M in the 1721AD nationwide shogunal census before plateauing near 33,3M in 1868AD, with Edo becoming the largest metropolis in the world. Concurrently in Korea, Gojoseon, Han commanderies and Three Kingdoms consolidation (Goguryeo, Baekje, Silla and Gaya) carry peninsular population from 700k at 250BC to 3,6M at 668AD, expanding under Unified Silla and Goryeo to a mediaeval peak of 5,8M in 1200AD before Mongol shocks. Joseon Dynasty agricultural expansion carries population from 5,55M in 1392AD to 14,06M in 1591AD, before the catastrophic Imjin War (1592-1598AD) depresses numbers to 11,2M in 1600AD. Eighteenth-century recovery lifts Joseon numbers to 18,66M in 1750AD before nineteenth-century peasant revolts, epidemics and climatic distress reduce totals to 17,43M by 1910AD.

Section 4 bridges these early modern baselines with modern twentieth-century statistical enumerations. Meiji industrialisation carries Japanese population from 33,27M in 1868AD to 55,99M in the first modern 1920 national census and 73,36M in 1940AD. Across colonial Korea, Japanese cadastral surveys and modern public health accompany expansion from 17,25M in 1905AD to 25,95M in 1945AD alongside mass overseas migration. Post-1945 liberation, peninsular partition along the 38th parallel, and the devastating Korean War (1950-1953AD) leave South Korea at 20,45M and North Korea at 8,49M in 1953AD. In postwar Japan, rapid economic reconstruction and baby booms carry population to 104,67M in 1970AD and a historic peak of 128,06M in 2010AD before prolonged demographic ageing reduces numbers to 122,45M by 2026AD. In South Korea, rapid industrialisation and urbanisation carry population to 51,83M in 2020AD (stabilising at 51,82M in 2026AD), while North Korea recovers to 24,05M in the 2008 census and 26,65M in 2026AD. Combined population across the CASTLE domain expands from 66,56M in 1910AD to 98,48M in 1945AD, 115,94M in 1953AD, 171,8M in 1980AD, passes 203,85M in 2020AD, and stabilises at 200,92M in 2026AD. All thirteen constituent chapters contribute 221 sub-regional analytical masks and 10.507 catalogued settlements without boundary tears, urban step discontinuities or unharmonised toponymic duplications.

# Background

Historical demographic reconstructions for Korea and Japan confront three structural challenges: the physical contrast between an insular volcanic archipelago and a mountainous continental peninsula, the divergent documentary traditions of dynastic household registers, and the deep statistical disruptions caused by modern colonial mobilisation, wartime displacement and postwar ideological partition.

Over past decades, global historical demographic syntheses have relied on broad sub-continental tabulations compiled by Colin McEvedy and Richard Jones [@McEvedyJones1978], Angus Maddison [@Maddison2001], and Massimo Livi-Bacci. These classic compendia assigned uniform growth rates to modern political boundaries or aggregated East Asian islands into undifferentiated regional blocks. In the History Database of the Global Environment (HYDE 3.1 and HYDE 3.2), Kees Klein Goldewijk and colleagues made major progress by downscaling historical totals to a 5-arcminute grid from 10000BC to the present [@KleinGoldewijk2017]. HYDE combined urban point allocations with rural suitability weighting derived from coastlines, river networks, soil capability, terrain slope and climate envelopes.

Yet across the Japanese archipelago and the Korean peninsula, human settlement followed geographical and historical dynamics that top-down global downscaling cannot resolve from modern political entities alone:

First, insular and peninsular environments operated under distinct ecological and physical constraints. Across the Japanese archipelago (Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku, Hokkaido and the Ryukyu arc), rugged volcanic topography confined human habitation to narrow coastal plains, intramontane basins and fertile alluvial deltas (such as the Kanto, Nobi, Kinai, Tsukushi, Sendai and Echigo plains) [@Barnes2015Archaeology; @Imamura1996Prehistoric]. Steep mountain chains formed natural barriers that isolated regional drainage basins, creating localized microclimates and fostering decentralized maritime trade networks along the Seto Inland Sea, the Japan Sea coast and the Pacific littoral. In contrast, the Korean peninsula presents an asymmetric landform: the rugged Taebaek and Rangrim mountain ranges run along the eastern spine, forcing major river systems—the Amnok (Yalu), Taedong, Han, Geum and Yeongsan—to flow westwards into the shallow Yellow Sea, with only the Nakdong basin draining southwards towards the Korea Strait [@Barnes2015Archaeology; @Choe2002Mumun]. These broad western alluvial basins provided the primary focus for sedentary agricultural settlement, while the eastern coast remained narrow and mountainous. Top-down models that apply uniform spatial allocation parameters across both zones misallocate populations across steep divides or distort mountain-basin population ratios.

Second, the historical evidentiary record is divided among distinct scholarly and institutional traditions. Prehistoric settlement patterns must be recovered through archaeological site registries, radiocarbon dating databases, shellmound inventories and megalithic monument files [@Kudo2023JapanC14; @Crema2020Jomon; @Koyama1978Jomon; @Habu2004AncientJomon; @Oh2017KoreaC14; @Kim2021NeolithicKorea]. In Japan, classical Ritsuryo registers (*koseki*), Shosoin fiscal documents, Kamakura warrior surveys, the nationwide *Taiko kenchi* land surveys of Toyotomi Hideyoshi (1582-1598AD), and the triennial or sexennial *shumon aratamecho* (religious inquiry registers) of the Tokugawa shogunate recorded adult taxable units or temple-affiliated households [@Farris2006Medieval; @Farris2009DailyLife; @Hayami2001Historical; @Hayami2010Population; @Sekiyama1958Kinsei; @Kito2000Jinko]. In Korea, dynastic counts recorded in the *Samguk sagi*, *Samguk yusa*, *Goryeosa*, and the triennial *hogu* household returns of the Joseon Dynasty (*Joseon Wangjo Sillok*) recorded registered households and adult males bearing identification tablets (*hopae*) [@KwonShin1977Joseon; @Kwon1977Demography; @Kim2023Ancient]. In both realms, direct readings of registered taxpayers produce severe undercounts during periods of fiscal avoidance, administrative decay, or institutional exemptions for ruling elites, unfree labourers and monastic clergy.

Third, the modern statistical transition requires harmonising divergent national and colonial census systems. The Meiji government instituted the *jinshin-koseki* household registration in 1872AD, leading into the first modern scientifically conducted census on 1 October 1920 by the Statistics Bureau of Japan [@SBJ2021Census; @NSTAC2026SSDSE]. In Korea, late Joseon surveys gave way to Japanese colonial cadastral surveys (1910-1918AD) and quinquennial colonial censuses from 1925 to 1944AD. Following the 1945 liberation and the 1948 division of the peninsula, the Korean War (1950-1953AD) caused massive excess mortality, internal displacement and cross-border refugee flights. Since 1953AD, demographic records have diverged into two separate statistical universes: the comprehensive modern censuses conducted by Statistics Korea (KOSTAT) in the South [@KOSIS2021Census], and the state-directed administrative registrations and UNFPA-assisted national censuses (1993 and 2008AD) in the North [@EberstadtBanister1992; @Spoorenberg2012DPRK; @UNFPA2008DPRKCensus; @Buzo2022Dprk].

Project CASTLE resolves these structural obstacles through bottom-up catchment-level geostatistical modelling and exhaustive settlement gazetteers across all thirteen constituent modules, establishing an unbroken historical population record from 10000BC to 2026AD.

# Methodology

## Regional Partitioning and Chronological Architecture

Project CASTLE establishes a hierarchical spatial and chronological partition designed to preserve sub-regional accounting integrity across shifting dynastic boundaries, feudal domains and modern administrative reorganisations. The spatial domain encompasses 617.753 km² of terrestrial East Asia across Japan and Korea, divided into four chronological sections and thirteen modular chapters:

1. **Section 1: Prehistoric Korea and Japan (1 module, 10000BC to 250BC)**: Module 1 covers Prehistoric and Food Gathering Korea and Japan across fourteen environmental regions (five Korean river basins and nine Japanese island divisions), documenting post-glacial forager adaptations, Jomon pottery cultures, Chulmun hunter-fishers, Mumun dry-field and wet-rice agricultural revolutions, and early bronze-iron transitions.
2. **Section 2: Japan Historical (4 modules, 250BC to 1945AD)**: Tracing insular Japanese demography across four sequential historical eras:
   - *Yayoi and Kofun Japan (250BC to 650AD, 13 sub-regions)*: Covering the continental diffusion of wet-rice agriculture, bronze and iron metallurgy, regional chiefdoms, Yoshinogari and Karako-Kagi moated settlements, and the Yamato court's consolidation of the Kofun tumulus state (expanding from 120k to 4,5M) [@Barnes2015Archaeology; @Hudson1992Rice; @West2024Agentbased; @Imamura1996Prehistoric].
   - *Nara, Heian and Feudal Japan (650 to 1603AD, 11 sub-regions)*: Following the Ritsuryo Gokishichido circuit system, the construction of imperial grid capitals (Fujiwara-kyo, Heijo-kyo and Heian-kyo), the catastrophic 735AD-737AD smallpox epidemic crash [@Farris2006Medieval; @Farris2009DailyLife; @Kito2000Jinko], Heian estate decentralisation (*shoen*), Kamakura bakufu warrior governance with double-cropping agrarian revolutions, and Sengoku castle town commercialisation (reaching 12,27M by 1603AD).
   - *Tokugawa Japan, Ryukyu and Ezo (1603 to 1868AD, 11 sub-regions)*: Documenting the Pax Tokugawa under the Edo shogunate, seventeenth-century agrarian land reclamation (*shinden kaihatsu*), the triennial and sexennial nationwide shogunal censuses from 1721AD to 1846AD [@Hayami2001Historical; @Hayami2010Population; @Sekiyama1958Kinsei], Edo's expansion into a million-person metropolis, eighteenth-century famine plateaus, Ezochi Ainu trade relations [@Walker2001ConquestAinu], and the Ryukyu Kingdom [@Smits2019MaritimeRyukyu] (reaching 33,3M in 1868AD).
   - *Meiji and Imperial Japan (1868 to 1945AD, 47 prefectures)*: Covering the abolition of the han system, the 1872AD jinshin-koseki baseline, rapid industrialisation, public health modernization, the Tokaido urban corridor, and modern decennial censuses from 1920AD to 1940AD before wartime destruction (peaking at 73,36M in 1940AD).
3. **Section 3: Korea Historical (5 modules, 250BC to 1953AD)**: Tracing peninsular Korean demography across five sequential eras:
   - *Gojoseon, Commanderies and Three Kingdoms (250BC to 668AD, 8 sub-regions)*: Covering Gojoseon, Han commanderies (Lelang and Daifang), and the Three Kingdoms period (Goguryeo, Baekje, Silla and the Gaya confederacy), detailing agricultural expansion along the Han, Geum and Nakdong valleys (expanding from 700k to 3,6M) [@Nelson2017Mumun].
   - *Unified Silla and Goryeo Korea (668 to 1392AD, 8 sub-regions)*: Following Silla's unification of the central and southern peninsula, the nine-province administrative order (*guju*), the Gyeongju royal capital (peaking at 350k), the founding of the Goryeo Dynasty in 918AD with Gaegyeong (Kaesong) as capital, agricultural clearance along the western littoral, the 1231-1270AD Mongol invasion crises, and late Goryeo recovery (peaking at 5,8M in 1200AD and closing at 5,55M in 1392AD).
   - *Joseon Korea (1392 to 1910AD, 8 historical provinces)*: Documenting the establishment of Hanyang (Seoul) as capital, the consolidation of the eight-province system (*paldo*), King Sejong's agrarian surveys, population growth to 14,06M in 1591AD on the eve of the Imjin War (1592-1598AD) [@KwonShin1977Joseon; @Cha2009LivingStandards; @Kim2023Ancient], post-war depression to 11,2M in 1600AD, eighteenth-century agricultural recovery under Yeongjo to 18,66M in 1750AD, and nineteenth-century peasant distress (closing at 17,43M in 1910AD).
   - *Korea under Japanese Occupation (1905 to 1945AD, 13 colonial provinces)*: Covering Japanese protectorate and colonial rule, modern cadastral surveys (1910-1918AD), colonial public health, industrialisation along the Seoul-Busan and northern mineral axes, and population growth from 17,25M in 1905AD to 25,95M in 1945AD alongside mass migration to Manchuria and Japan.
   - *Korean Division and Korean War (1945 to 1953AD, 13 provinces)*: Documenting post-liberation repatriation, division along the 38th parallel, the 1949 Republic of Korea census, and the catastrophic Korean War (1950-1953AD) involving heavy military and civilian casualties and massive refugee flight across the Demilitarized Zone (closing at 28,94M in 1953AD: South Korea 20,45M, North Korea 8,49M).
4. **Section 4: Modern Censuses (3 modules, 1945/1953 to 2026AD)**: Uniting contemporary statistical reporting across the three modern polities:
   - *Postwar and Contemporary Japan (1945 to 2026AD, 47 prefectures)*: Tracking post-war reconstruction, the 1947-1949 baby boom, rapid industrialisation along the Pacific Coast belt, population expansion from 72,53M in 1945AD to 104,67M in 1970AD, peaking at 128,06M in 2010AD, and subsequent rapid ageing to 122,45M in 2026AD across all 47 prefectures [@SBJ2021Census; @NSTAC2026SSDSE].
   - *Republic of Korea after 1953 (1953 to 2026AD, 17 administrative divisions)*: Tracking the Miracle on the Han River, rapid rural-to-urban migration, massive concentration in the Seoul Capital Area (Sudogwon), fertility decline, and population expansion from 20,45M in 1953AD to 51,83M in 2020AD, stabilising at 51,82M in 2026AD [@KOSIS2021Census].
   - *Democratic People's Republic of Korea after 1953 (1953 to 2026AD, 11 provincial units)*: Tracking post-war socialist reconstruction, industrialisation in Pyongyang, Hamhung and Chongjin, growth from 8,49M in 1953AD to 21,21M in 1993AD, the 1995-2000AD famine crisis (*Arduous March*), the UNFPA-assisted 2008 census (24,05M), and slow expansion to 26,65M in 2026AD [@EberstadtBanister1992; @Spoorenberg2012DPRK; @UNFPA2008DPRKCensus; @Buzo2022Dprk].

Together, the thirteen modules incorporate 221 sub-regional analytical masks that cover every square kilometre of Japan and Korea without jurisdictional gaps or spatial overlaps.

## Archaeological Substrata and Non-Stationary Matérn Kriging

Prehistoric and early historical rural settlement potential across the 9.224 valid terrestrial 5-arcminute cells (617.753 km²) of Project CASTLE is derived from a massive compilation of archaeological excavations, radiocarbon registers, shellmound inventories, ancient tumuli records and administrative gazetteers. The database consolidates 103.888 composite site-epoch records across nine chronological horizons, incorporating:
- Comprehensive radiocarbon compilations for Japan, including Kudo et al. (2023) and Crema and Kobayashi (2020) [@Kudo2023JapanC14; @Crema2020Jomon];
- Korean prehistoric radiocarbon inventories, including Oh et al. (2017) and Kim et al. (2021) [@Oh2017KoreaC14; @Kim2021NeolithicKorea];
- National archaeological gazetteers from the Agency for Cultural Affairs of Japan and the National Research Institute of Cultural Heritage of Korea;
- Harvard CHGIS Version 6 frontier buffer records along the Korean-Manchurian border [@Barnes2015Archaeology];
- Comprehensive historical settlement registers and ancient toponymic databases covering Kofun burial mounds, Yayoi moated villages, Mumun dolmen fields, Ritsuryo post stations, Joseon local administrative seats (*eupchi*), and Tokugawa post stations (*shukuba*).

The nine chronological horizons span the full developmental sequence of human occupation across the Japanese archipelago and the Korean peninsula:
- Horizon 1 (Palaeolithic, Incipient to Early Jomon and Chulmun, c. 13000BC to 3500BC): Microblade industries, Incipient Jomon cord-marked pottery, Gosan-ri and Osan-ri early coastal shellmounds (mean intensity 5,32, active cells 9.123);
- Horizon 2 (Middle Jomon and Chulmun, c. 3500BC to 2500BC): Middle Jomon climax villages in central and northeastern Honshu (Sannai-Maruyama, Kasori) and Korean peninsular riverine sites (Amsa-dong) (mean intensity 4,27, active cells 9.123);
- Horizon 3 (Late to Final Jomon, Mumun and Bronze Age, c. 2500BC to 300BC): Kamegaoka culture in Tohoku, Mumun intensive dry-field and wet-rice agricultural settlements, Songguk-ri and Daepyeong-ri pit dwellings, and megalithic dolmen concentrations (mean intensity 4,06, active cells 9.123);
- Horizon 4 (Yayoi, Gojoseon and Han Commanderies, c. 300BC to 300AD): Continental wet-rice paddy field networks in northern Kyushu and Setouchi (Yoshinogari, Karako-Kagi), Gojoseon fortified towns, and Lelang and Daifang commandery seats along the Taedong and Han valleys (mean intensity 6, active cells 9.123);
- Horizon 5 (Kofun and Three Kingdoms, c. 300AD to 668AD): Keyhole-shaped burial tumuli (*zenpokoenfun*) across the Kinai core (Mozu-Furuichi) and Kanto, alongside royal capitals and mountain fortresses of Goguryeo (Pyongyang), Baekje (Hanseong, Ungjin, Sabi/Buyeo), Silla (Gyeongju), and Gaya (mean intensity 5,12, active cells 9.123);
- Horizon 6 (Asuka, Nara, Early Heian and Unified Silla, c. 668AD to 900AD): Imperial grid capitals (Fujiwara-kyo, Heijo-kyo, Heian-kyo), provincial administrative seats (*kokufu*), and Unified Silla nine-province administrative centres and Gyeongju metropolis (mean intensity 4,16, active cells 9.123);
- Horizon 7 (Late Heian, Kamakura and Goryeo Dynasty, c. 900AD to 1392AD): Kamakura warrior residences, *shoen* estate centres, Goryeo capital Gaegyeong (Kaesong), celadon production centres, and Buddhist temple estates (mean intensity 3,52, active cells 9.123);
- Horizon 8 (Muromachi, Sengoku and Early Joseon, c. 1392AD to 1603AD): Sengoku castle towns (*jokamachi*), port cities (Sakai, Hakata), Hanyang (Seoul) royal capital wall, and early Joseon local magistrate seats (mean intensity 3,47, active cells 9.123);
- Horizon 9 (Edo, Late Joseon and Modern Era, c. 1603AD to 1910AD): Tokugawa castle town networks, post stations along the Five Routes (*Gokaido*), Osaka commercial wards, Joseon *eupchi* county seats, and market towns (*jangsi*) (mean intensity 3,28, active cells 9.123).

To eliminate arbitrary modern political boundary distortions, the spatial domain is partitioned using HydroBASINS Level 6 watershed units, comprising 383 active domestic catchments (out of 384 total domestic catchments, representing an administrative coverage ratio of 0,9974). The median Voronoi catchment radius is 25,09 km, with a 90th percentile of 28,32 km.

Geostatistical interpolation relies on a two-dimensional Paciorek and Schervish non-stationary Matérn covariance kernel with fixed smoothness $\nu = 3/2$ [@Paciorek2006Matern]. The spatial covariance between two locations $s_i$ and $s_j$ is given by:
$$C(s_i, s_j) = \sigma^2 |\Sigma_i|^{1/4} |\Sigma_j|^{1/4} \left|\frac{\Sigma_i + \Sigma_j}{2}\right|^{-1/2} \left(1 + \frac{\sqrt{3} Q_{ij}}{\tau}\right) \exp\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3} Q_{ij}}{\tau}\right)$$
where $Q_{ij} = \sqrt{(s_i - s_j)^T \left(\frac{\Sigma_i + \Sigma_j}{2}\right)^{-1} (s_i - s_j)}$, and $\Sigma_i$ represents the locally adaptive spatial metric tensor aligned to river valley orientation, coastline proximity and terrain slope.

Residual kriging operates on top of five weighted least squares biophysical covariates: baseline habitation suitability ($\beta_0$), terrain slope suitability ($\beta_1$), ecozone agricultural productivity ($\beta_2$), distance decay from primary river channels ($\beta_3$, 12,5 km characteristic decay scale), and distance decay from marine coastlines ($\beta_4$, 25 km decay scale). Weighted least squares fitting across all nine horizons yields variogram parameters with $\tau_1 = 1,4211$ and macro scale range $\tau_2 = 2,6291$.

## Dynastic Cadastres and Modern Statistical Continuities

For historical periods following classical state formation, CASTLE synthesises empirical household and cadastral returns by drawing on foundational demographic scholarship for Japan and Korea [@Kito2000Jinko; @Farris2006Medieval; @Hayami2001Historical; @Sekiyama1958Kinsei; @KwonShin1977Joseon; @Kwon1977Demography; @Cha2009LivingStandards].

Pre-modern censuses in Japan and Korea were fiscal and administrative registration systems designed to assess corvée labour obligations, military levies, agricultural tribute and religious orthodoxy rather than statistical headcounts. In Japan, classical Ritsuryo *koseki* registers omitted absconders, infants and unfree servile classes. The *shumon aratamecho* instituted by the Tokugawa shogunate in the 1630s to suppress Christianity became a nationwide population survey conducted every six years between 1721AD and 1846AD [@Hayami2001Historical; @Sekiyama1958Kinsei]. However, these registers routinely excluded samurai elites, shogunal direct retainers (*hatamoto* and *gokenin*), their domestic servants, imperial court nobles in Kyoto, Buddhist and Shinto priests, and outcast communities (*eta* and *hinin*), requiring systematic upward adjustments of eight to ten per cent to recover total de facto population [@Hayami2010Population].

In Korea, the triennial household registers (*hogu*) of the Joseon Dynasty and the civil identity tablet system (*hopae*) instituted under King Taejong suffered from pervasive under-registration [@KwonShin1977Joseon]. Landlords and local lineages concealed dependent peasant households (*nobi*) and tenant cultivators to evade corvée labour and military grain taxes (*gunpo*). Kwon and Shin (1977) established that official Joseon registered headcounts recorded only thirty-five to fifty per cent of actual living inhabitants. CASTLE adopts Kwon and Shin's demographic adjustment factors, calibrated against sex ratios, lineage genealogies (*jokbo*), agricultural rice productivity series, and local gazetteers [@Cha2009LivingStandards].

From 1868AD onward, CASTLE links these dynastic baselines to modern scientific censuses. In Japan, the 1872AD *jinshin-koseki* household registration established the modern statistical foundation (34,7M), connecting through late Meiji police surveys to the landmark first modern national census of 1 October 1920 (55,99M) conducted by the Statistics Bureau of Japan [@SBJ2021Census; @NSTAC2026SSDSE]. In Korea, late Joseon enumerations connect with Japanese colonial cadastral surveys (1910-1918AD) and colonial quinquennial censuses from 1925 to 1944AD. Following the 1945 liberation and the 1950-1953AD Korean War, continuous decennial and quinquennial censuses conducted by Statistics Korea (KOSTAT) provide an unbroken record for South Korea [@KOSIS2021Census]. For North Korea, the 1993 and 2008 national censuses conducted in collaboration with the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), analysed by Eberstadt and Banister (1992) and Spoorenberg and Schwekendiek (2012), provide the statistical backbone, with military population adjustments and post-2008 demographic projections carrying numbers to 2026AD [@EberstadtBanister1992; @Spoorenberg2012DPRK; @UNFPA2008DPRKCensus].

## Urban Agglomeration and Settlement Gazetteers

Urban settlements across Project CASTLE are catalogued in discrete gazetteer archives encompassing 10.507 distinct settlement records. Each settlement carries permanent composite identifiers, WGS84 geographic coordinates, native script toponyms (Kanji and Kana for Japan; Hanja and Hangul for Korea), foundation dates, administrative ranks and historical population trajectories.

To prevent urban populations from being double-counted within rural agricultural pixels, CASTLE implements an urban disaggregation algorithm:
1. Urban settlement points are buffered according to their historical rank and physical extent (3 km to 15 km buffer radius) and projected onto the 5-arcminute raster grid;
2. Settlement populations at each benchmark year are assigned directly to the corresponding urban grid cells;
3. Urban pixel totals are subtracted from their respective sub-regional population targets, yielding residual rural population totals;
4. Residual rural populations are disaggregated across non-urban pixels using the normalised non-stationary Matérn kriging suitability weights;
5. A two-pass separable Gaussian filter smoothing kernel eliminates seam discontinuities across administrative borders while preserving sub-regional totals.

Annual live continuity outside verified border splice years (1868, 1905, 1910, 1945 and 1953AD) is enforced through constrained monotonic cubic Hermite splines, maintaining year-on-year aggregate turnover below 1,5% and preventing artificial statistical jumps during intercensal intervals.

# Testing and Validation

Project CASTLE enforces five orthogonal validation checks across all thirteen constituent chapters:

1. **Areal Mask Integrity**: All thirteen modular masks contain zero empty sub-regions, zero synthetic bounding-box cuts, and complete territorial containment across 221 sub-regional analytical units covering 617.753 km². Explicit polygon boundaries enclose coastal islands including Tsushima, Iki, Sado, Oki, the Goto Archipelago, the Ryukyu-Amami Arc, Jeju Island, Ulleungdo and Ganghwa Island without raster clipping errors.
2. **Kriging Sharpness and Continuity**: Across all nine Holocene horizons, variograms achieve regularised $\tau_1 = 1,4211$ and $\tau_2 = 2,6291$, with an effective median Voronoi radius of 25,09 km. Visual inspection confirms sharp fluvial and coastal alignment along the Tone, Shinano, Yodo, Kiso, Chikugo, Han, Nakdong, Geum, Taedong and Amnok river systems, with zero isotropic Voronoi artefacts and complete suppression of uninhabitable alpine ridges in the Japanese Alps and the northern Korean highlands.
3. **Gazetteer Deduplication and Coverage**: All 10.507 catalogued settlements pass coordinate bounds checks, parent sub-region containment, and pairwise proximity audits (zero same-jurisdiction active settlement pairs within 1,5 km after 1850AD).
4. **Toponymic Disambiguation and Anti-Collision Protection**: Historical toponymic shifts are systematically resolved. The model distinguishes historical capitals from modern administrative cities, isolating ancient Asuka, Fujiwara-kyo and Heijo-kyo (Nara) from Heian-kyo and modern Kyoto, separating Edo from modern Tokyo, distinguishing Hanyang and Gyeongseong from modern Seoul, separating Gaegyeong from modern Kaesong, and isolating ancient Geumseong from modern Gyeongju.
5. **Continuity and Visual Inspection**: Annual live continuity checks confirm that year-on-year population changes remain within demographic viability bounds. All project-level diagnostic figures pass optical inspection for zero label occlusion, proper aspect ratio and publication-grade cartographic clarity.

# Results

## Prehistoric Demography and Forager Transitions in Korea and Japan

The demographic history of the Japanese archipelago and the Korean peninsula between 10000BC and 250BC illustrates how post-glacial environmental conditions shaped distinct hunter-gatherer adaptations and divergent pathways to food production (Figure \ref{fig:trajectory}) [@Habu2004AncientJomon; @Kim2021NeolithicKorea; @Oh2017KoreaC14; @Koyama1978Jomon].

<figure class="crd-figure-block" id="fig:trajectory">
<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_castle/1.0/fig2_castle_long_run_trajectory.png" alt="fig:trajectory" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 3.</span> Long-run population trajectories of Japan (10000BC to 2026AD) and Korea (10000BC to 2026AD) on logarithmic scales, illustrating dynastic cycles, agricultural transitions and modern demographic changes.</figcaption>
</figure>

At the close of the Last Glacial Maximum (10000BC), small mobile bands of Upper Palaeolithic and Incipient Jomon foragers occupied the coastal margins and river valleys of Japan and Korea, supporting an aggregate domain population of approximately 32k (Japan 20k, Korea 12k) [@Morisaki2025More; @Kudo2023JapanC14]. During the Holocene Climatic Optimum (6000BC to 3000BC), warming temperatures expanded rich temperate deciduous forests dominated by nut-bearing oaks, chestnuts and walnuts (*Castanea* and *Quercus*) across central and northeastern Honshu, while maritime marine resources flourished along the shallow coastal rias of both the archipelago and the peninsula [@Crema2020Jomon; @Habu2004AncientJomon].

In Japan, this ecological bounty sustained the Middle Jomon culture (c. 3500BC to 2500BC), characterised by substantial sedentary pit-dwelling villages (such as Sannai-Maruyama in Aomori and the massive Kasori shellmounds in Chiba), sophisticated ceramic vessels, and intensive plant management [@Habu2004AncientJomon; @Crema2016Summed]. Japanese population reached a mid-Holocene peak of 261k around 3000BC, with over seventy per cent concentrated in the central highlands of Chubu and the Kanto and Tohoku regions [@Koyama1978Jomon]. In Korea, contemporary Chulmun hunter-fishers settled along major river mouths (Amsa-dong on the Han River) and coastal shellmounds (Dongsam-dong in Busan), sustaining an estimated 110k inhabitants by 3000BC [@Kim2021NeolithicKorea; @Oh2017KoreaC14].

Between 2500BC and 1500BC, global climatic cooling reduced forest nut yields, triggering severe population contractions across eastern Japan, where numbers dropped to 160k by 1000BC [@Crema2020Jomon; @Koyama1978Jomon]. In contrast, the Korean peninsula underwent a decisive economic transformation with the emergence of the Mumun pottery culture (c. 1500BC to 300BC). Mumun communities cleared broad alluvial terraces along the Han, Geum and Nakdong valleys, introducing intensive dry-field farming of foxtail millet, broomcorn millet, barley, wheat and soybeans, alongside early wet-rice cultivation [@Choe2002Mumun; @Lee2011Archaeological; @Leipe2017Barley]. Large nucleated settlements (such as Songguk-ri in Buyeo and Daepyeong-ri in Jinju) and thousands of megalithic dolmen burials reflect increasing social stratification and rapid demographic expansion, carrying peninsular population to 700k by 250BC [@Barnes2015Archaeology; @Choe2002Mumun]. Combined domain population reached 820k in 250BC as western Japan prepared for the continental arrival of Yayoi wet-rice agriculture (120k).

## Ancient State Formation, Commanderies and Three Kingdoms

Between 250BC and 668AD, the diffusion of irrigated wet-rice agriculture, bronze and iron metallurgy, and continental statecraft transformed both insular Japan and peninsular Korea from tribal chiefdoms into centralised monarchies [@Barnes2015Archaeology; @Imamura1996Prehistoric; @Nelson2017Mumun].

In Japan, the Yayoi period (c. 300BC to 300AD) began with the arrival of continental farming migrants across the Korea Strait into northern Kyushu, bringing irrigated paddy technology, iron tools and bronze ritual objects [@West2024Agentbased; @Hudson1992Rice]. Wet-rice farming expanded rapidly along the Seto Inland Sea into the Kinai plain and the Tokai basin, multiplying local carrying capacity. Population grew at an annual rate exceeding 0,4%, rising from 120k in 250BC to 600k at 1AD, 1,2M in 200AD, and 1,8M by 300AD. Nucleated moated settlements (such as Yoshinogari in Saga and Karako-Kagi in Nara) gave way to regional political confederations. During the subsequent Kofun period (300 to 650AD), the Yamato polity unified the Kinai basin, mobilizing vast labour reserves to construct massive keyhole-shaped burial tumuli, notably the Daisenryo Kofun (Emperor Nintoku) in the Mozu-Furuichi cluster [@Barnes2015Archaeology]. By 650AD, Japanese population reached 4,5M.

In Korea, the Early Iron Age witnessed the expansion of Gojoseon and the establishment of the four Han commanderies (notably Lelang and Daifang) following the Han conquest in 108BC. Chinese commandery administrative registers recorded over 400k registered inhabitants in Lelang commandery in 2AD, reflecting substantial immigration from the Chinese Central Plains. Concurrently, southern indigenous societies organised into the Samhan confederacies (Mahan, Jinhan and Byeonhan), developing intensive wetland rice farming along the Yeongsan and Nakdong basins. By 300AD, these chiefdoms coalesced into the Three Kingdoms: Goguryeo in the north, Baekje in the southwest, Silla in the southeast, and the Gaya confederacy in the lower Nakdong basin [@Nelson2017Mumun]. Between 300AD and 668AD, military competition spurred agricultural improvements, reservoir construction and mountain fortress building, lifting peninsular population from 2,2M in 300AD to 3,6M in 668AD on the eve of Silla's unification of the southern peninsula.

## Mediaeval Dynasties, Agrarian Revolutions and Urban Networks

The mediaeval era (650AD to 1603AD) witnessed state centralisation, demographic crises from epidemic diseases, and agrarian expansion driven by technological innovation.

In Japan, the Asuka and Nara periods established the Ritsuryo legal system, laying out Chinese-style grid capitals at Fujiwara-kyo and Heijo-kyo (Nara) with populations reaching 70k to 100k [@Farris2009DailyLife; @Kito2000Jinko]. Between 735AD and 737AD, a virulent smallpox epidemic introduced from the Asian mainland swept through the archipelago, killing an estimated twenty-five to thirty-five per cent of the total population, including senior members of the ruling Fujiwara clan [@Farris2006Medieval; @Farris2009DailyLife; @Kito2000Jinko]. Japanese population collapsed from 5,4M in 730AD to 4M in 740AD, prompting the imperial court to issue the 743AD Law of Perpetual Land Ownership (*Konden Einen Shizai Ho*) to stimulate private land reclamation. Slow recovery under the Heian court (peaking at 6,5M around 1000AD) was followed by the rise of the warrior class (*bushi*) and the founding of the Kamakura bakufu in 1185AD. The mediaeval agricultural revolution—characterised by double-cropping of rice and barley, iron-tipped plows, draught animals, night-soil fertilisation, and water wheels—carried Japanese population to 7M in 1200AD, 9,6M in 1400AD, and 12,27M by 1603AD amidst Sengoku castle town urbanisation (Sakai, Hakata, Odawara and Osaka) [@Farris2006Medieval].

In Korea, Silla's unification in 668AD established an enduring peninsular political core. Under Unified Silla (668 to 935AD), peace and agricultural stability supported 3,85M in 700AD and 4,2M in 750AD, with the capital Gyeongju (*Geumseong*) expanding into a grand metropolis of 350k inhabitants [@Nelson2017Mumun]. Following the founding of the Goryeo Dynasty in 918AD, the new capital Gaegyeong (Kaesong) flourished as a maritime commercial centre of 260k people. Goryeo population expanded from 4,5M in 1000AD to a mediaeval zenith of 5,8M in 1200AD. The devastating Mongol invasions between 1231AD and 1270AD caused widespread destruction, siege starvation and depopulation, reducing peninsular numbers to 4,3M by 1260AD. Agricultural recovery under late Goryeo restored population to 5,55M by 1392AD.

## Early Modern Consolidation: Tokugawa Japan and Joseon Korea

The early modern era witnessed the establishment of long periods of internal peace: the Tokugawa shogunate in Japan (1603 to 1868AD) and the Joseon Dynasty in Korea (1392 to 1910AD).

In Joseon Korea, founding ruler Taejo established Hanyang (Seoul) as capital, enclosing it with a 18,6 km fortress wall. Under King Sejong (reigned 1418-1450AD), scientific rain gauges (*cheugugi*), agrarian treatises (*Nongsa jikseol*), and reservoir maintenance stimulated agricultural expansion [@Kim2023Ancient]. Peninsular population rose from 5,55M in 1392AD to 14,06M in 1591AD on the eve of the Japanese invasions launched by Toyotomi Hideyoshi [@KwonShin1977Joseon; @Cha2009LivingStandards]. The catastrophic Imjin War (1592-1598AD), followed by the Manchu invasions of 1627AD and 1636AD, devastated the country through battlefield mortality, mass starvation, disease and the destruction of cadastral and irrigation records. Total population dropped by over twenty per cent to 11,2M in 1600AD and 11,6M in 1637AD. Under the eighteenth-century reigns of Yeongjo and Jeongjo, agricultural recovery, the spread of transplanting techniques (*iangbeop*), and commercial market networks (*jangsi*) lifted population to an early modern peak of 18,66M in 1750AD [@KwonShin1977Joseon]. During the nineteenth century, repeated cholera epidemics, monsoon floods, corrupt taxation (*samjeong mundran*), and peasant uprisings (such as the 1811 Hong Gyeong-nae rebellion and the 1894 Donghak peasant war) caused demographic stagnation, leaving population at 16,48M in 1850AD and 17,43M in 1910AD.

In Tokugawa Japan, victory at Sekigahara in 1600AD inaugurated two and a half centuries of Pax Tokugawa [@Hayami2001Historical]. Between 1603AD and 1721AD, peaceful conditions, extensive shogunal and domainal land reclamation projects (*shinden kaihatsu*), and commercialisation along the Tokaido and Seto Inland Sea sparked an unprecedented population surge. Japanese population expanded from 12,27M in 1603AD to 27,69M in 1700AD and 31,28M in 1721AD, when the eighth shogun Tokugawa Yoshimune mandated the first nationwide census [@Hayami2010Population; @Sekiyama1958Kinsei]. Edo expanded into a metropolis exceeding one million inhabitants, while Osaka served as the national commercial clearinghouse (*tenka no daidokoro*) and Kyoto remained the cultural and craft capital. Between 1721AD and 1846AD, population plateaued between 29,8M and 32,3M due to periodic climatic cooling and catastrophic famines (the Kyoho famine of 1732AD, the Tenmei famine of 1782-1788AD, and the Tenpo famine of 1833-1837AD) alongside widespread rural family limitation practices (*mabiki*) [@Hayami2001Historical]. By the 1868AD Meiji Restoration, Japanese population stood at 33,3M.

## Industrialisation, Imperial Expansion and Colonial Mobilisation

Between 1868AD and 1945AD, East Asia underwent profound political, economic and military transformations.

Following the Meiji Restoration, Japan modernised rapidly through railway construction, textile industrialisation, modern public health, and compulsory primary education. Population grew at an accelerating pace, rising from 33,27M in 1868AD to 43,72M in 1900AD, 55,99M in the first modern 1920 national census, and a peak of 73,36M in 1940AD [@SBJ2021Census]. Urbanisation concentrated millions into the Keihin (Tokyo-Yokohama), Hanshin (Osaka-Kobe) and Chukyo (Nagoya) industrial belts. Wartime mobilization, overseas military casualties, Allied aerial bombing campaigns, and naval blockades reduced population to 72,53M by late 1945AD.

In Korea, Japanese colonial rule (1910 to 1945AD) imposed modern cadastral surveys (1910-1918AD), rice extraction policies (*Sanmi jeungsik gyehoek*), and colonial public health measures. Peninsular population expanded from 17,25M in 1905AD to 19,52M in 1925AD, 24,33M in 1940AD, and 25,95M in 1945AD. Rapid domestic growth was accompanied by massive outward migration: over two million Koreans moved to Manchuria and the Russian Far East, while more than two million labourers and conscripts were mobilised to work in mines and factories across the Japanese home islands.

## Postwar Partition, Reconstruction and Modern Demographic Realignment

Following the surrender of Japan in August 1945, the Korean peninsula was divided along the 38th parallel into American and Soviet occupation zones. The outbreak of the Korean War (1950 to 1953AD) caused immense destruction across both halves of the peninsula. Over two million soldiers and civilians died, and more than one million refugees fled from north to south across the 38th parallel and the eventual Demilitarized Zone (DMZ). By the 1953 armistice, South Korea's population stood at 20,45M, while North Korea's population stood at 8,49M (peninsular total 28,94M).

Over the seven decades since the 1953 armistice, both polities experienced dramatic economic and demographic transformations (Figure \ref{fig:urban-hierarchy}).

<figure class="crd-figure-block" id="fig:urban-hierarchy">
<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_castle/1.0/fig4_castle_urban_hierarchy.png" alt="fig:urban-hierarchy" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 4.</span> Urban settlement hierarchies across historical epochs and contemporary Korea and Japan: rank-size distributions and major urban agglomerations led by Tokyo, Seoul and Osaka.</figcaption>
</figure>

In postwar Japan, rapid reconstruction, the return of 6,2M overseas military personnel and civilian repatriates, and the 1947-1949 baby boom propelled population from 72,53M in 1945AD to 84,11M in 1950AD and 104,67M in 1970AD [@SBJ2021Census]. The economic miracle cemented the Tokaido megalopolis as the dominant urban axis. Population reached a historic peak of 128,06M in the 2010 census before fertility decline and rapid population ageing reduced numbers to 126,15M in 2020AD and 122,45M in 2026AD [@NSTAC2026SSDSE].

In South Korea, post-war economic modernisation (the Miracle on the Han River) triggered rapid rural-to-urban migration and a classic demographic transition. Population doubled from 20,45M in 1953AD to 40,42M in 1985AD, passing 50M in 2012AD and reaching a peak of 51,83M in the 2020 census, before ultra-low total fertility rates (falling below 0,75 births per woman) brought population to 51,82M in 2026AD [@KOSIS2021Census]. Over half of South Korea's population became concentrated in the Seoul Capital Area (Sudogwon).

In North Korea, post-war socialist reconstruction and heavy industrialisation propelled population from 8,49M in 1953AD to 14,62M in 1970AD and 21,21M in the 1993 census [@EberstadtBanister1992]. In the mid-1990s, the collapse of Soviet aid, consecutive floods and droughts, and economic contraction caused the catastrophic Arduous March famine (1995 to 2000AD), resulting in an estimated 300k to 600k excess deaths and widespread child stunting [@Spoorenberg2012DPRK; @Buzo2022Dprk]. Slow recovery documented in the UNFPA-assisted 2008 census (24,05M) carried population to 26,65M by 2026AD [@UNFPA2008DPRKCensus].

# Discussion

## Comparison with Global Baselines

Contrasting Project CASTLE against earlier global reconstructions—notably the History Database of the Global Environment (HYDE 3.1 and HYDE 3.2) [@KleinGoldewijk2017], Angus Maddison's historical accounts [@Maddison2001], and Colin McEvedy and Richard Jones's atlas [@McEvedyJones1978]—reveals major methodological and empirical divergences.

Table \ref{tab:global-comparison} contrasts Project CASTLE macro totals against these three global compilations across key historical benchmarks from 1000BC to 1950AD.

Three structural differences distinguish CASTLE from earlier global syntheses:

First, **amplitude of dynastic cycles and epidemic crises**: Global compilations such as HYDE and Maddison apply monotonic or smoothed demographic curves between widely separated benchmark years, dampening the real amplitude of dynastic expansions and catastrophic transition collapses. In 750AD, HYDE and McEvedy assume approximately 6M to 6,2M across Japan and Korea; CASTLE establishes 8,5M (Japan 4,3M, Korea 4,2M), incorporating the sharp 735AD-737AD smallpox epidemic mortality documented by Farris (2006, 2009) and Kito (2000) that temporarily dropped Japanese population from 5,4M to 4M [@Farris2006Medieval; @Farris2009DailyLife; @Kito2000Jinko]. Around 1200AD, global baselines estimate 9M to 9,5M, whereas CASTLE documents 12,8M (Japan 7M, Korea 5,8M) driven by the mediaeval double-cropping agricultural revolution in Japan and high Goryeo agrarian clearance in Korea. In 1600AD, global baselines overlook the catastrophic mortality of the Imjin War (1592-1598AD) in Korea, which reduced peninsular numbers from 14,06M in 1591AD to 11,2M in 1600AD. Around 1750AD, global baselines underestimate combined totals at 35,5M to 38M, whereas CASTLE demonstrates 49,76M based on the 1721-1846AD Tokugawa nationwide shogunal censuses (31,1M) and Kwon and Shin's adjusted Joseon dynastic baseline (18,66M) [@Hayami2001Historical; @Sekiyama1958Kinsei; @KwonShin1977Joseon].

Second, **spatial distribution and terrain constraints**: Top-down downscaling models rely on modern land-cover, road network and city distributions to disaggregate historical population, creating pervasive backward-projection bias. In HYDE 3.2, substantial populations appear in the low-lying Kanto delta and northern Hokkaido during classical antiquity. CASTLE's non-stationary Matérn kriging substrata anchor population to verified archaeological and epigraphic find-spots, keeping Middle Jomon population clustered in the central highlands of Chubu and Kanto, Yayoi population clustered in northern Kyushu and Setouchi, and Three Kingdoms population concentrated in the Han, Geum and Nakdong basins, while suppressing high-altitude alpine crags.

Third, **settlement granularity and urban continuity**: Global urban databases (such as Chandler 1987 and Modelski 2003) adopted arbitrary city thresholds (such as 20k or 40k inhabitants), omitting the thousands of castle towns (*jokamachi*), post stations (*shukuba*), port settlements, and Korean county seats (*eupchi*) that formed the real backbone of East Asian urbanism. By compiling 10.507 settlements with continuous trajectories from each chapter's gazetteer archive, CASTLE eliminates the artificial twentieth-century urban step discontinuities that occur when small towns enter tabular compilations for the first time.

## Methodological Limitations

Four primary methodological limitations should be considered when utilizing Project CASTLE outputs:

First, archaeological sampling intensity varies across ecological and economic zones. In lowland agricultural basins and modern metropolitan regions (Tokyo, Osaka, Nagoya and Seoul), intense modern infrastructure construction and salvage archaeology have generated tens of thousands of excavated loci, whereas survey density is sparser in the high volcanic cordilleras of central Honshu, Hokkaido taiga, and the northern mountains of Hamgyong and Chagang. While the use of HydroBASINS Level 6 catchments, biophysical covariates and Poisson-Gamma shrinkage damps these survey gradients, residual coverage disparities remain.

Second, dynastic household registers vary in recording criteria across regimes. The conversion of registered households (*hu* or *koseki*) and taxable adults into total de facto population requires estimating household dependency ratios, unregistered dependents, and female omissions. Although CASTLE follows the established standards developed by Hayami, Kito, Kwon and Shin, confidence intervals widen for chaotic transition intervals such as the Sengoku period in Japan and the post-Imjin recovery in Korea.

Third, colonial and wartime statistical dislocations complicate early twentieth-century reconstructions. Japanese colonial cadastres in Korea from 1910 to 1918AD altered landholding definitions, while wartime censorship and statistical confidentiality during World War II (1944-1945) obscure fine-scale prefectural totals. During the Korean War (1950 to 1953AD), massive displacement and the destruction of local archives create uncertainty regarding the exact geographical distribution of excess mortality.

Fourth, contemporary demographic data accessibility diverges between the open statistical systems of Japan (Statistics Bureau of Japan) and South Korea (KOSTAT) versus the centralised administrative system of North Korea. In the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, researchers must rely on the 1993 and 2008 UNFPA-assisted censuses and indirect demographic projections, requiring careful cross-validation with satellite imagery, agricultural output data and refugee demographic reports.

## Conclusion

Project CASTLE establishes an empirical, spatially continuous demographic reconstruction of the Japanese archipelago and the Korean peninsula from 10000BC to 2026AD. By synthesising 103.888 composite archaeological site observations, nine non-stationary Matérn kriging horizons, authoritative dynastic cadastral records, and modern statistical censuses across 221 sub-regions and 10.507 catalogued settlements, CASTLE overcomes the distortions of earlier top-down continental models.

The resulting dataset provides an open, geostatistically documented baseline for comparative long-run studies of human adaptation, environmental transformation, urbanisation and demographic cycles across Korea and Japan.
